extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, tertiary mathematics instructors, and mathematics-education researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and empirically-tested criteria for presenting mathematical proofs to undergraduate students to maximize pedagogical clarity and usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: H1: explicit hypothesis and conclusion statements (introductory/concluding sentences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians believe that a proof may be more easily understood by undergraduates when it contains hypothesis and conclusion statements that make explicit what is being accomplished in the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding an introductory sentence provides a 'roadmap' and lets students know explicitly what is being proved; it can also remind students of relevant definitions (e.g., the definition of injectivity). Some participants found the concluding sentence less helpful or superfluous, so introductory (goal-setting) statements are more consistently beneficial than explicit concluding sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: H2: emphasize main ideas by formatting key equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians believe that emphasizing the main ideas used in a proof (for example, by reformatting key formulas) can improve its pedagogical quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place significant equations on their own line and center them or otherwise increase spacing to draw attention. Benefits reported include making the proof less cluttered, easier to read, and visually highlighting where the main ideas occur. Note: some of the perceived benefit may be purely visual/readability (spacing) rather than conceptual emphasis; consider both effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: H3: add justifications when students cannot be expected to infer them
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians believe that adding extra justifications to support an assertion can improve the clarity of a proof if that justification might be difficult for a student to infer on their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extra justification to bridge logical gaps that undergraduates may find challenging. However, there is substantial disagreement: some view added justification as helpful and preventing confusion, while others view it as unnecessary lengthening or clutter. Authors should weigh the perceived difficulty of the inference for their specific audience; there is tension between clarity and conciseness.

rubrics_metrics.name: H4: avoid unnecessary or irrelevant calculations and assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians agree that including unnecessary, irrelevant computations or assumptions in a proof will lower its pedagogical quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unnecessary calculations/assumptions lengthen proofs, distract or confuse readers, and may lead students to wonder why the material was included. Examples from the study: adding an irrelevant calculation that is not used later, or inserting an extraneous assumption (e.g., 'f is real-valued') that diverts attention from salient hypotheses. Remove material that is not germane to the main ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual appearance, spacing, and readability matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual layout choices (spacing, uncluttered lines, displayed equations) are valued because they make proofs easier to read and recall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improving visual appearance—greater spacing, avoiding cramped inline formulae, centering pivotal equations—makes proofs psychologically easier on the eyes and more appealing, which contributes to pedagogical value. Formatting choices that increase readability are therefore pedagogically relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor level of detail to audience capability
rubrics_metrics.description: There is not universal agreement among mathematicians about what inferences undergraduates should be able to make; therefore the appropriate level of detail depends on the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to include intermediate steps or justifications based on the expected capabilities of the intended students. Including steps may prevent confusion for some students but may be perceived as clutter by others; instructors must balance providing scaffolding against promoting student-inference and concision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a simple evaluative scale for judging modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: In the study, participants judged modified proofs using a five-point scale: 'significantly better', 'somewhat better', 'the proofs were the same', 'somewhat worse', 'significantly worse'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For quantitative evaluation of presentation changes, code responses as 2 (significantly better), 1 (somewhat better), 0 (same), -1 (somewhat worse), -2 (significantly worse). Allow optional free-text comments to capture nuanced rationales (e.g., 'roadmap' benefit, distraction by added assumption).
